title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Identify the multi-gear shaft assembly's primary function.
student: What is the primary mechanical function of the multi-gear shaft assembly?
instructor: The shaft supports the mounted gears and transfers rotational power and torque between different stages of the drive system. The bearings support and align the rotating shaft.
gradingNotes: Students should describe the physical power-transmission role before using the analytical labels from the instructor model.

title: External Mechanical Loading
learningObjectives: Identify the mechanical loading applied by the mounted gears.
student: What type of mechanical loading do the mounted gears apply to the shaft during power transmission?
instructor: The gears apply torques to the shaft. Depending on the direction of power flow at a gear location, a gear may introduce torque into the shaft or remove torque from it.
gradingNotes: The base problem considers torsion only; transverse gear forces and gear weights are excluded.

title: Supports and Bearings
learningObjectives: Explain the bearing role in the physical and idealized systems.
student: What is the mechanical role of the shaft bearings in the real assembly?
instructor: The bearings support and align the rotating shaft while permitting rotation. In the simplified torsion model, ideal frictionless bearings do not resist torque about the shaft axis.

title: Torque Transfer Through the Shaft
learningObjectives: Predict how internal torque varies along a multi-gear shaft.
student: How would you expect the torque carried by the shaft to change as power is introduced or removed at different gear locations?
instructor: The internal torque changes when a gear applies or removes torque. Different portions of the shaft can therefore carry different torque magnitudes and even different torque signs.

title: Critical Shaft Region
learningObjectives: Identify the condition governing torsional shear stress in a constant-diameter shaft.
student: For a constant-diameter shaft, what determines which portion of the shaft experiences the largest torsional shear stress?
instructor: The portion carrying the largest magnitude of internal torque experiences the largest torsional shear stress, provided the shaft diameter is the same throughout.

title: Relevant Design Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify the parameters governing shaft stress and hollow-shaft design.
student: What geometric and mechanical characteristics would influence torsional stress and the design of a hollow replacement shaft?
instructor: Relevant characteristics include the magnitudes and directions of the applied torques, shaft outer diameter, wall thickness or inner diameter, and allowable shear stress. Material shear modulus would also be relevant if angle of twist were evaluated.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Create a simplified multi-gear shaft model.
student: Convert the real multi-gear shaft assembly into a simplified Mechanics of Materials model. Show the shaft axis, gear locations, bearing locations, applied torque directions, shaft segments, and shaft diameter. Establish a positive torque sign convention.
instructor: A correct idealization represents the system as a circular shaft with concentrated torques applied at the gear locations and ideal bearings that support the shaft but do not resist shaft-axis torque.
gradingNotes: Detailed gear-tooth geometry and transverse loading are not required in the torsion model. Students should attempt their own idealization before using the instructor reference figure.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State the assumptions used in the simplified torsion model.
student: State the assumptions used to convert the physical drive system into the simplified torsion model.
instructor: The shaft is circular and prismatic; the material is homogeneous and linearly elastic; gear torques are represented as concentrated torques; bearings do not resist shaft-axis torque; deformation is small; warping and local stress concentrations are neglected; and transverse gear forces, bending, fatigue, and dynamic effects are excluded from the base model.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the complete shaft evaluation and redesign procedure.
student: Before performing numerical work, describe the analysis sequence needed to evaluate the existing shaft and size the hollow replacement.
instructor: Choose a torque sign convention; verify overall torque equilibrium; determine the internal torque in each shaft segment; construct the torque diagram; calculate torsional shear stress in each solid-shaft segment; identify the governing torque; derive the hollow-shaft sizing relation; select a practical wall thickness by rounding upward; and verify the selected design.

title: Torque Sign Convention and Overall Equilibrium
student: Using the instructor reference diagram, select a positive torque direction and verify overall torque equilibrium.
instructor: Using the assigned convention: TB = +40, TC = -60, TD = -30, and TF = +50 kN·m. Therefore, ΣT = {{gear_torque_sum_kNm}} kN·m. {{gear_equilibrium_assessment}}
gradingNotes: Any consistent sign convention is acceptable if all subsequent segment torques are treated consistently.

title: Internal Torque in Each Segment
learningObjectives: Determine the internal torque in every shaft segment.
student: Determine the signed internal torque and magnitude in shaft segments AB, BC, CD, DE, and EF.
instructor: TAB = {{gear_T_AB_kNm}} kN·m, TBC = {{gear_T_BC_kNm}} kN·m, TCD = {{gear_T_CD_kNm}} kN·m, TDE = {{gear_T_DE_kNm}} kN·m, and TEF = {{gear_T_EF_kNm}} kN·m. The magnitudes are {{gear_abs_T_AB_kNm}}, {{gear_abs_T_BC_kNm}}, {{gear_abs_T_CD_kNm}}, {{gear_abs_T_DE_kNm}}, and {{gear_abs_T_EF_kNm}} kN·m.

title: Internal Torque Diagram
learningObjectives: Construct and interpret the internal torque diagram.
student: Construct the internal torque diagram along the shaft and identify each jump.
instructor: The diagram is zero on AB, jumps by +40 kN·m at B, changes by -60 kN·m at C, changes by -30 kN·m at D, remains unchanged through bearing E, and changes by +50 kN·m at F to return to zero.
gradingNotes: An ideal bearing does not introduce a torque jump.

title: Maximum Shear Stress in the Existing Solid Shaft
learningObjectives: Calculate maximum torsional shear stress in every shaft segment.
student: For d = 160 mm, calculate the maximum torsional shear stress in every shaft segment.
instructor: For a solid circular shaft, τmax = 16|T|/(πd3). The segment stresses are: AB = {{gear_tau_AB_MPa}} MPa; BC = {{gear_tau_BC_MPa}} MPa; CD = {{gear_tau_CD_MPa}} MPa; DE = {{gear_tau_DE_MPa}} MPa; and EF = {{gear_tau_EF_MPa}} MPa.
gradingNotes: Use torque in N·mm and diameter in mm.

title: Governing Segment
learningObjectives: Identify the shaft segment controlling the hollow-shaft sizing.
student: Identify the governing shaft segment or segments and explain why they control the hollow-shaft sizing.
instructor: {{gear_governing_segments}} {{gear_governing_verb}} because each carries |T| = {{gear_governing_torque_kNm}} kN·m, the largest internal torque magnitude. Since the solid shaft has uniform diameter, these locations also have the largest torsional shear stress.

title: Hollow-Shaft Sizing Equation
learningObjectives: Derive the hollow-shaft allowable-stress sizing equation.
student: For a hollow shaft with outer diameter Do = 160 mm and allowable shear stress of 90 MPa, derive the equation used to determine the largest permissible inner diameter.

title: Minimum Wall Thickness
learningObjectives: Calculate and select the minimum practical wall thickness.
student: Determine the theoretical minimum wall thickness and select a practical whole-millimeter thickness.
instructor: Di,max = {{gear_D_i_max_mm}} mm. Therefore, tmin = (160 - Di,max)/2 = {{gear_t_min_mm}} mm. Because a minimum thickness cannot be rounded downward, select t = {{gear_t_selected_mm}} mm.

title: Verification of Selected Thickness
learningObjectives: Verify the selected hollow-shaft wall thickness.
student: Recalculate the maximum shear stress using the selected wall thickness of 21 mm.
instructor: The inner diameter is Di = 160 - 2(21) = {{gear_D_i_selected_mm}} mm. Using the governing torque of 50 kN·m gives τmax = {{gear_tau_selected_MPa}} MPa, which is below the 90 MPa allowable stress. The utilization is {{gear_utilization}}. {{gear_thickness_assessment}}

title: Engineering Interpretation
learningObjectives: Explain torque-diagram continuity across an ideal bearing.
student: Explain why the bearing at E does not create a jump in the torque diagram and why segments DE and EF carry the same torque.
instructor: An ideal bearing supports the shaft transversely but does not apply torque about the shaft axis. The internal torque therefore remains unchanged across E until the external torque at gear F is encountered.

title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
student: Using the preceding mechanics results, provide a concise recommendation for the hollow-shaft replacement and identify the main limitations of the simplified analysis.
instructor:
{{gear_recommendation}}

The hollow design reduces material and rotating mass while retaining adequate torsional strength under the stated model. A detailed industrial design would additionally consider transverse gear forces and bending, combined stress, fatigue, keyways and shoulders, deflection, bearing loads, critical speed, manufacturing tolerances, and dynamic torque fluctuations.
gradingNotes: The final recommendation should remain limited to the pure-torsion model rather than claiming complete gearbox design acceptance.
